issues.legal_issue: Tribal customary succession rules should not be declared unconstitutional in the abstract without examination of the particular custom and its effects.
material_facts: The petitions challenged succession rules affecting tribal communities whose customary practices and views about inheritance differed from those under generally applicable personal laws.
The State reported that tribal representatives opposed changing the rules because of concerns about alienation of tribal land and community disruption.
The court considered that imposing other communities’ personal-law principles on tribal communities through judicial action would disregard those differences.
issues.conclusion: The court declined to declare tribal customs offending Articles 14, 15 and 21, stating that each case must be examined on its full facts.
issues.legal_principle: Constitutional equality does not require every community to have uniform succession rules, and differences in succession treatment do not invariably violate Article 14. Courts should exercise restraint in applying other communities’ personal laws to tribal customs or creating a uniform succession scheme through judicial action. The court agreed with the approach in the opinion of K. Ramaswamy, J., while emphasizing that particular cases must be assessed on their facts.

predicates.tribal_customary_succession_case: The proceeding challenges succession practices followed by a tribal community.
predicates.community_customs_materially_differ: The community follows inheritance customs that differ from those applied to other communities.
predicates.effects_of_the_particular_custom_are_not: The court does not have a full examination of the particular custom and its effects in the case before it.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns tribal customary succession and community differences or the effects of the particular custom remain material, the custom is not declared unconstitutional without case-specific examination.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory references to male-line descendants cannot be judicially read as granting female descendants equal statutory succession rights.
material_facts: The challenged provisions identified certain tenancy classes and, for the relevant classes, referred to male-line descendants.
The provisions concerned the identification and regulation of tenancy rights, not ownership of the land.

A prior High Court decision had allowed a widow to retain tenancy possession during her lifetime, but the court found that decision had overlooked part of the statutory definition and was decided on its facts.
issues.conclusion: The court held that sections 7 and 8 could not be read down to include female descendants alongside male descendants as equal statutory heirs.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 7 and 8 of the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act define particular tenancy interests and use male-line language; they do not establish ownership succession rules that can be rewritten to confer equal statutory inheritance. The court distinguished Jitmohan Singh Munda v. Ramratan Singh and Another, finding it was not a guiding precedent for reading female descendants into section 8. It also considered that the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and the Indian Succession Act, 1925 did not apply to the relevant Scheduled Tribes by default, referring to section 2(2) of the former and section 3 of the latter.

predicates.statutory_tenancy_succession_case: The proceeding concerns statutory provisions governing succession to a particular tenancy interest.
predicates.provisions_define_tenancy_classes: The relevant provisions classify or define tenancy interests rather than ownership of land generally.
predicates.provisions_specify_male_line_descendants: The provisions identify male-line descendants as persons included in the relevant statutory class.

issues.definition: Where a succession proceeding concerns provisions defining tenancy classes and specifying male-line descendants, female descendants are not read into those provisions as equal statutory heirs.

issues.legal_issue: A female dependent or descendant of the last male holder may retain the holding while she depends on it for her livelihood, suspending exclusive male succession during that dependence.
material_facts: The statutory scheme provided for succession in the male line to the relevant tenancy interests.
Female relatives of a deceased male holder could be dependent on the land and could lose their means of livelihood if required to leave it in favour of a male successor.
The court treated the right to livelihood as part of the right to life and considered the agricultural work performed by members of the holder’s family.
issues.conclusion: The court held that female dependents or descendants could continue to hold the land while they remained dependent on it for their livelihood; male successors could take exclusive possession when those women exhausted or abandoned that means of livelihood. The court directed the State to examine possible legislative change and the related exemptions from succession legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, as explained in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation. Articles 39(a), 41 and 37 inform the understanding of that right. The court therefore recognized a limited, intervening right for female dependents or descendants under sections 7 and 8, without striking those provisions down: exclusive male succession remains suspended while a qualifying woman depends on the holding for livelihood, and may operate when she abandons or no longer needs it for that purpose.

predicates.tribal_tenancy_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns succession to a tenancy interest governed by a tribal community’s statutory and customary setting.
predicates.female_relative_of_last_male_holder: A woman is a dependent or descendant of the last male holder of the tenancy.
predicates.depends_on_holding_for_livelihood: The woman relies on the holding as a means of earning her livelihood.

issues.definition: In a tribal tenancy succession dispute, a female relative of the last male holder who relies on the holding for livelihood may retain it while that dependence continues.
